help: top:
usage: poisson-trace [-h] [--version] [--plain] VERB ...

Poisson Trace reads the runs Prove has stored and says where in the workflow their episodes
died, and whether a change made them fail less. A store is the folder Prove writes its runs
into; a run is one stored sweep, and its episodes are its rows. Every number prints with what
the runs could not have detected.

A run is named by a name you gave it with poisson-trace name; by the name it has from its
manifest, the record Prove keeps of it (its target, the day it started in UTC and a letter, such
as "tau2-airline 2026-09-15 a"); by latest or previous, the newest complete runs, or
latest:TARGET and previous:TARGET, a target's ("latest:tau2-airline"); by its number in the
runs listing ("#3"); or by its full id.

Results another tool wrote (DeepEval, Ragas, a table of results, JUnit reports) are read in
with poisson-trace import. where, compare, fix-check and changes also take a folder in a run's
place, when no stored run answers to the word: a run Prove stored, a store of one run, or one
tool's result files, read with the flags poisson-trace import takes for that tool. Nothing is
written; the folder's name is the run's name in the report.

To begin, run poisson-trace init: it finds the results already here, asks what counts as a
failure and writes trace.toml, from which every verb then takes its store and its failures.
Then poisson-trace doctor says whether this environment is ready.

options:
  -h, --help   show this help message and exit
  --version    print the versions of Trace, Prove and Python
  --plain      print plain text with no colour, as on a pipe; may come before
               or after the verb

verbs:
  VERB
    init       guided setup: finds your results, asks what counts as a
               failure, writes trace.toml
    runs       the runs of a store, newest first, with their names and numbers
    name       give a stored run a name of yours, take it back, or list the
               names
    where      where in the workflow the episodes of one stored run died
    compare    a before (A) and an after (B), compared
    fix-check  an old and a new version re-run on the same inputs, compared
    changes    the inputs whose failure share moved between two runs
    import     read in the results another tool wrote, as one new run of a
               store
    doctor     whether this environment is ready, and what to run when it is
               not
    handover   check a handover bundle --out wrote: every file, digest and
               promised key

examples:
  poisson-trace runs --store proofload-runs --event unsolved
  poisson-trace where previous --store proofload-runs --event unsolved --at 20
  poisson-trace fix-check previous latest --store proofload-runs --event unsolved \
      --inputs all --max-mde 0.2

# Poisson Trace · fix check · agent before (old) and agent after (new)

## Summary

- Compared: old agent before against new agent after, on the same 4 inputs: 160 tries of each. A try counts as failed when it ended timeout or violated.
- Question: Did the new version fail more or less often than the old? You asked that the run be able to catch a 10-point drop in how often it fails.
- Answer: Fewer failures, if tries of an input count as independent (here they are fairly alike). The new version failed 41 of 160 tries and the old 72 of 160 (19 fewer per 100 tries); 31 of the net 31 fewer failures come from task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55.
- Next: Run both versions side by side on these inputs with your own harness, then run `poisson-trace fix-check` on the two new runs.

## Before you act on this

- They started 2 s apart. Trace can't tell whether they were run side by side, so anything else that changed between them (the provider, the model behind the API, the day) may be part of the difference, in either direction.
- Both runs name the same target (mock-agent); Trace can't tell what differs between them, only what you tell it.
- These results fit anything from 12 to 27 fewer failures per 100 tries, but that range is only a rough guide here and may be off either way (fewer than 10 inputs vary): don't use it to rule sizes in or out.
- Tries of the same input are counted as separate chances; here they are fairly alike (agreement 0.61, where 0 is no more alike than chance and 1 is identical), and if they are near copies the answer is more confident than it should be.
- If each input failed equally often under both versions, a gap at least this big, either way, would turn up less than once in 1,000 (counting tries as independent).
- A check of which inputs went up and which went down can't rule out chance on its own (p = 0.500 in the report), so the gap rests on task_id refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55. Without task_id refund at tool_fail_rate 0.55 and task_id search at tool_fail_rate 0.55, the gap is 0.00 points (p = 1.00).
- Before putting the difference down to the version, run both side by side.

## The two versions

## The comparison

exact conditional Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, stratified by input over 4 inputs (2 informative), two-sided; α = 0.05.

new failures: observed 41, expected 56.500, variance 7.073; p = 3.62e-09
difference: -19.4 points, new minus old (-27.4 to -12.3; Mantel-Haenszel weights; range: stratified Miettinen-Nurminen score interval, 95%, for these inputs as run; rough here: fewer than 10 inputs vary)
by input: p = 0.500 (sign-flip over the 2 inputs that moved, exact); not part of the line below

## Consistency

failure share 0.353 · fails again 0.750 · κ 0.613 · within-input variance 0.088 against pooled 0.228
a comparison that ignored the inputs would need 1/(1 − κ) = 2.58 times the runs

## What it could not have detected

proportional change on every input, 80% power, α = 0.05, continuity-corrected normal approximation to the stratified statistic.

- a drop in failure share: could not have detected one below 10.9 points
- a rise in failure share: could not have detected one below 11.7 points

**different: the new version failed less on these inputs (exact Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel, stratified by input, p = 3.62e-09)**

## Inputs that changed

Fisher's exact test per input, Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05 over 4 inputs; 2 flagged.

| input | old failed/runs | new failed/runs | change | p | q | flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| {"task_id":"search","tool_fail_rate":0.55} | 32/40 | 10/40 | -55.0 points | 1.45e-06 | 5.80e-06 | failed less in new |
| {"task_id":"refund","tool_fail_rate":0.55} | 40/40 | 31/40 | -22.5 points | 0.002 | 0.005 | failed less in new |
| {"task_id":"refund","tool_fail_rate":0.0} | 0/40 | 0/40 | 0.0 points | 1.000 | 1.000 | – |
| {"task_id":"search","tool_fail_rate":0.0} | 0/40 | 0/40 | 0.0 points | 1.000 | 1.000 | – |

A lone changed input is flagged only if its p is below α / M = 0.0125, and the smallest p an input of this design can give is 1.86e-23: a lone change can be flagged; a lone complete flip needs 5 repeats per arm. An input with no flag is not an input that did not change.

## What this cannot say

- A difference between two stored runs is a difference between the runs. The version, the provider and the hour changed together unless the two were run side by side, and this test cannot separate them.
- Repeat runs of one input are read as separate draws and never as replays: a served model is not bit-identical on repeat, so nothing here matches a run of the old version to a run of the new by seed.
- If repeat runs of one input are near copies of one another, the run-level test overstates its confidence. The by-input line does not depend on that.
- Rows with no outcome are left out of both arms and counted in the header. A new version that times out where the old one failed does not show as a failure here.
- Trace reads the runs it is given. If the inputs were chosen by the old arm's own outcomes, or the more favourable of several runs was handed over, the confidence printed does not hold.
- The detection limit and the run counts are computed from these runs' own failure rates, which are estimates. They are a guide to the next design, not a promise about it.
